question: The Spanish Government, through the Foundation for the Internationalisation of Public Administration (FIAP), has promoted the creation of two migrant detention centres in Mauritania.

An investigation by El Salto1 reveals that its construction and equipment were financed with Spanish and EU public funds under both the European Union Emergency Trust Fund for Africa and the Common Operational Partnership, a police cooperation project coordinated by FIAP.

The purpose of those centres is to arbitrarily detain migrants and asylum seekers in conditions that do not fall under either its oversight or the application of legal guarantees. The use of EU funds to build detention centres in non-EU countries violates Articles 2, 3 and 78 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, as well as the Charter of Fundamental Rights. 1.
Is this initiative part of the EU’s border externalisation policy?
What safeguards are in place to guarantee the right to seek asylum?
‘Spanish Government opens two migrant prisons in Mauritania’, El Salto, 5 November 2025, https://www.elsaltodiario.com/fronteras/gobierno-espana-abre-dos-carceles-migrantes-mauritania.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.5.2026) As part of the strengthened partnership between the Islamic Republic of Mauritania and the EU1, the EU has supported the rehabilitation and equipment of Mauritania’s two temporary migrant reception centres (CATE) in Nouakchott and Nouadhibou, via the Common Operational Partnership coordinated by Foundation for the Internationalisation of Public Administration.

The rehabilitation of the Nouakchott centre was completed in October 2025, followed in January 2026 by the Nouadhibou centre. The EU is currently supporting the functioning of both centres through two projects, whose main aim is to ensure the presence of international organisations2, and to enable them to provide services to migrants and advice to Mauritanian authorities.

These centres cannot be used to detain migrants arrested by the authorities3; their mandate instead is to provide dignified shelter and immediate assistance after disembarkation to migrants rescued at sea by Mauritanian authorities4.

They also offer a structured space for individual screening to determine these migrants’ legal status in Mauritania and identify those in need of international protection or special assistance5, who must receive specific protection in Mauritania and are exempt from forced return. Safeguards are in place to guarantee fundamental rights. Migrants can stay in these centres for maximum 72 hours.

Children are admitted into the centres only when they are accompanied by family members. The individual assessment of each disembarked migrant is carried out by Mauritanian authorities, with the support of the International Organization for Migration and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees.
The National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights have permanent access for monitoring. The CNDH co-manages the complaints mechanism.
1 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/eu-mauritania-joint-declaration_en. 2 The International Organization for Migration, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees and the International

Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent. 3 EU Delegation to Mauritania’s press release, 24 November 2025 (in French and in Spanish): https://www.eeas.europa.eu/delegations/mauritanie/communiqu%C3%A9-de-la-d%C3%A9l%C3%A9gation-del%E2%80%99union-europ%C3%A9enne-en-mauritanie_fr?s=109. 4 https://www.interieur.gov.mr/fr/node/459. 5 Including minors, pregnant women, victims of trafficking, persons with disabilities or medical conditions, and other vulnerable persons.
